clinicalPearls: Most viral gastroenteritis is caused by RNA viruses, but DNA enteric adenoviruses (types 40 and 41) are also recognized causes; the principal pathogens are rotavirus, norovirus, sapovirus, astrovirus, and enteric adenovirus.

Illness presents with acute onset of vomiting and/or diarrhea, often with fever, nausea, abdominal cramps, anorexia, and malaise; the diarrhea is characteristically watery and nonbloody, without mucus or fecal leukocytes.

Norovirus has become the leading cause of medically attended gastroenteritis in young children in the United States and other developed countries following the decline in severe rotavirus disease after routine rotavirus vaccination, and it affects all age groups.

Norovirus is responsible for roughly half of all reported gastroenteritis outbreaks in the United States and is the major cause of gastroenteritis epidemics worldwide; it also causes traveler's diarrhea and outbreaks among deployed military personnel.

The infectious dose for most viral agents is very low (about 10-100 viral particles), in contrast to the higher inoculum typically required for many bacterial pathogens; norovirus can spread by fecal-oral route, aerosolization of vomitus, contaminated fomites, and person-to-person contact.

Nearly all children worldwide are infected with rotavirus by 3-5 years of age; first symptomatic infection usually occurs after 3 months of age, disease incidence peaks at 4-23 months, and severity decreases with each repeat infection.

Protection against rotavirus correlates with virus-specific secretory IgA in the intestine (and to some degree serum); because intestinal IgA is short-lived, full protection is temporary, but successive reinfections build progressively greater immunity.

Susceptibility to norovirus is influenced by host genetics: histo-blood group antigen (HBGA) phenotype and secretor status affect attachment, and functional antibodies that block norovirus binding to HBGAs correlate with protective immunity.

Rotavirus antigenemia and viremia are common in acutely infected children, although serum antigen and RNA levels are far lower than stool levels; rotavirus is shed in very large quantities in stool (10^7-10^12 per gram).

In temperate climates viral gastroenteritis shows winter seasonality, whereas in tropical/year-round settings seasonal peaks are less pronounced; before vaccination, US rotavirus season began in the Southwest in autumn/early winter and migrated to peak in the Northeast in late winter/spring.
Fever is common with both rotavirus and norovirus but uncommon with the other viral agents; up to one-third of rotavirus patients may have a temperature above 39 degrees C.

Death is a rare outcome and usually results from severe dehydration in vulnerable hosts such as debilitated elderly patients and young children; acute gastroenteritis is a leading cause of childhood death in developing countries (roughly 0.5 million deaths annually) and a major cause of pediatric hospitalization (6-8%) in industrialized nations.
harrison.pathophysiology: Enteric viruses injure the small-intestinal mucosa to produce predominantly watery diarrhea. With human caliciviruses (Norwalk/norovirus), carbohydrates resembling human histo-blood group antigens on the gastroduodenal epithelium of secretor-phenotype individuals appear to serve as attachment ligands; infection causes reversible lesions of the upper jejunum with broadening and blunting of villi, microvillar shortening, epithelial vacuolization, crypt hyperplasia, and lamina propria infiltration by neutrophils and lymphocytes. These changes persist for at least 4 days after symptom resolution and produce malabsorption of carbohydrates and fats with reduced brush-border enzymes; adenylate cyclase activity is unchanged. No histopathologic change occurs in stomach or colon, but delayed gastric motor function is thought to drive the characteristic nausea and vomiting. Rotavirus infects and destroys mature enterocytes of the proximal small-intestinal villous epithelium; loss of absorptive cells plus proliferation of secretory crypt cells yields secretory diarrhea, while reduced brush-border enzymes leave unmetabolized disaccharides that cause osmotic diarrhea. The nonstructural rotavirus protein NSP4 acts as an enterotoxin altering epithelial permeability and function, and rotavirus may also stimulate fluid secretion via activation of the enteric nervous system.
additionalDifferentials: Bacterial gastroenteritis (e.g., Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Vibrio cholerae, enterotoxigenic E. coli) - distinguished by inflammatory/bloody diarrhea, fecal leukocytes, and epidemiologic features
Preformed bacterial toxin food poisoning (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus) - very short incubation of hours
infectionMimics: Bacterial enteritis (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter jejuni, Vibrio, E. coli)
Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus cereus preformed-toxin food poisoning
Gastrointestinal symptoms of systemic respiratory viral infections (SARS-CoV, influenza A/H5N1, pandemic influenza A/H1N1)
nonInfectiousMimics: Osmotic or secretory diarrhea from other causes
Other causes of acute vomiting without true gastroenteritis
additionalInvestigations: Commercial enzyme immunoassays (EIA) for rotavirus and enteric adenovirus in stool
RT-PCR / multiplex molecular panels for norovirus and other enteric pathogens (increasingly used clinically)
Electron microscopy and polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) for viral RNA - largely research/public-health tools
Fecal examination for leukocytes and blood to help separate viral (typically negative) from inflammatory bacterial causes
Stool culture on special media when bacterial pathogens are suspected
redFlags: Signs of severe dehydration (especially in young children and debilitated elderly)
Inability to tolerate oral intake due to frequent vomiting
Bloody diarrhea or fecal leukocytes - should prompt evaluation for a bacterial/inflammatory cause rather than viral gastroenteritis
Protracted diarrhea with prolonged viral excretion or systemic dissemination in severely immunocompromised hosts (e.g., post-bone-marrow transplant rotavirus disease)
harrison.prognosis: Viral gastroenteritis is generally self-limited. Human calicivirus illness has a sudden onset after a mean incubation of about 24 hours (range 12-72 h) and typically lasts 12-60 h; norovirus and sapovirus illness usually resolves in 1-3 days. Rotavirus illness begins abruptly after a 1-3 day incubation, with vomiting often preceding diarrhea, and gastrointestinal symptoms generally resolve in 3-7 days. Among healthy young adults the illness is rarely fatal but causes substantial morbidity and lost work time. The main serious complication is dehydration; death is uncommon and concentrated in the very young, the elderly, and those with debilitating conditions. Severely immunodeficient children may develop protracted rotavirus diarrhea with prolonged shedding and, rarely, systemic dissemination.
pitfalls: Distinguishing viral from bacterial gastroenteritis on clinical and epidemiologic grounds alone is often unreliable; laboratory testing may be needed, and viral gastroenteritis is frequently a diagnosis of exclusion in practice.
Antibiotics and antimotility agents are inappropriate for viral gastroenteritis and are contraindicated.
Commercial stool EIA kits for norovirus have limited sensitivity and are most useful in outbreak investigation (many specimens tested) rather than for diagnosing individual patients.

Higher preexisting antibody to Norwalk virus does not guarantee protection - early studies paradoxically found higher antibody levels associated with greater susceptibility, later explained by host HBGA genetics rather than simple antibody titer.

Rotavirus has been associated with diverse conditions (SIDS, necrotizing enterocolitis, intussusception, Kawasaki disease, type 1 diabetes) and with respiratory/neurologic features, but no causal relationship has been confirmed for any of these.

Asymptomatically infected and pre-symptomatic persons can shed norovirus, and shedding can persist for weeks after recovery (prolonged in immunocompromised hosts), so a single negative or positive result must be interpreted with care.
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not provide a formal grading scale; clinical severity is described per agent and ranges from subclinical/mild infection to severe gastroenteritis with life-threatening dehydration. Relative clinical severity by virus: group A rotavirus is the most severe (predominantly children under 5), norovirus is moderate (all ages), and sapovirus, astrovirus, and enteric adenovirus are generally milder (mainly children under 5).
management: Oral rehydration solution to correct and prevent dehydration is the mainstay, with intravenous fluids reserved for severe dehydration or failed oral intake
Early resumption of normal feeding and continued breastfeeding, with zinc supplementation in young children in resource-limited settings
Selective antiemetic such as ondansetron to facilitate oral rehydration in vomiting children, avoiding routine antidiarrhoeal and antibiotic use
Monitor hydration status and correct electrolyte disturbances arising from fluid losses
Infection control with strict hand hygiene, contact isolation and exclusion from work or school, particularly for norovirus outbreaks
Rotavirus immunisation of infants for prevention
Escalate for intravenous rehydration when dehydration is severe or oral intake cannot be maintained
